summary: Santosh Radha introduces Covalent, an open-source product by Agnostiq designed to let developers write Python locally and seamlessly ship code to any compute backend. The core mechanism is a single decorator added above a Python function in a Jupyter notebook, specifying desired compute resources such as GPU type (e.g., H100), memory, and maximum runtime. The code is dispatched to a backend—either the user's own compute cluster or Covalent's cloud GPU cluster—and results return to the local notebook. Users pay only for actual GPU time consumed. Covalent also supports inference deployment: users define initializer functions and endpoints (e.g., /generate) as Python functions, then call a single deploy command. The service scales to zero or up based on custom auto-scaling rules defined by the user (time-based, GPU utilization thresholds, request counts), all without touching Docker or Kubernetes. The live demo shows a workflow that loops over multiple models to fine-tune, evaluates accuracy on GPU machines, sorts models on CPU-only machines to avoid wasting GPU resources, and deploys the best-performing model as a scalable inference endpoint. Example costs cited include 87 cents for a 6-minute L4 evaluation run and 11 cents for a 6-minute V100 run. Additional examples available via QR code include real-time time series analysis, transformer-based time series models, NER systems, LLM serving, and building an AI model foundry entirely in Python.

takeaways: Covalent lets you run Python functions on remote GPUs by adding a single decorator specifying compute resources, with no Kubernetes or Docker required.
Users pay only for actual GPU time consumed—e.g., 5 minutes of H100 usage costs only 5 minutes of billing.
You can bring your own compute cluster (cloud or on-prem) or use Covalent's managed cloud GPU cluster.
Inference deployment is fully Pythonic: define Python functions, call a single deploy command, and receive a scalable API endpoint with custom auto-scaling rules.

Sorting and evaluation tasks are routed to CPU-only machines to avoid wasting GPU resources.

sections.title: Introduction and Covalent Overview
sections.summary: Santosh introduces the talk about running compute easily from Python, aiming to showcase fine-tuning many models without Kubernetes or Docker. He explains Covalent, an open-source product that lets users write Python locally and ship code to any compute backend via a single decorator specifying GPU type, memory, and time limits. Users can bring their own compute or use Covalent's cloud cluster, paying only for actual GPU time used.

sections.title: Inference and Auto-Scaling Features
sections.summary: Covalent supports inference deployment entirely in Python. Users define initializer and endpoint functions (e.g., /generate), call a single deploy command, and receive a scalable API endpoint. Custom auto-scaling can be configured by time, GPU utilization, or request count. No Docker or Kubernetes interaction is required. Additional examples are available via a linked QR code, including time series analysis, transformer models, NER systems, and building an AI model foundry.

sections.title: Live Demo: Fine-Tuning Workflow
sections.summary: The demo walks through defining Python tasks with decorators: a fine-tune function running on a 24-core CPU with one H100 GPU (48 GB, 18-hour limit), an evaluation task, a sorting task on CPU-only machines, and a deployment task with a /generate endpoint. A workflow loops over multiple models, fine-tunes each, evaluates, sorts by accuracy, and deploys the best model—all dispatched via a single line of code.

sections.title: Demo Results and Costs
sections.summary: The Covalent application UI shows individual jobs running on different hardware with costs and runtimes. An L4 evaluation run took 6 minutes and cost 87 cents; a V100 run took 6 minutes and cost 11 cents. Santosh concludes that the entire process—fine-tuning, evaluation, and deployment—was accomplished in Python without Docker or Kubernetes, and invites attendees to visit the Covalent booth for more discussion.
